title: Target Narrative in a Controlled Trial to Localize Company‑First → Orchestration Drift
description: Produce a concise internal brief and trial plan that treats Narrative as the primary controlled variable to test whether and how it contributes to company‑first → orchestration reframing. The deliverable will (a) summarize Experiment 010’s finding that Narrative is the most recurrent first visible locus while explicitly noting Idea and Synthesis also caused drift in some runs, (b) propose a single controlled upstream‑boundary trial that holds reconstructed source, Idea, Research and Synthesis prompts constant and varies Narrative per a clear rule, (c) define pass/fail criteria across three evaluation axes (factual fidelity, company‑first hierarchy, editorial quality), and (d) include only stage text that Experiment 010 preserves: use quoted phrases already present in the report tables (e.g., “orchestration‑first,” “reliably converts,” “predictable and repeatable”) and, if longer excerpts are required, extract them only from the run artifacts listed in experiment-010’s evidence-manifest.json with exact file paths and hashes cited. Frame the document as an evidence‑based experiment design and not as a guaranteed fix.
audience: Nuëyon.Compose experiment designers, prompt engineers, product/content leads and evaluators who will run and judge the controlled trial.
rationale: Experiment 010 identifies Narrative as the most recurrent first visible hierarchy shift but explicitly cautions it is not always the origin (Idea and Synthesis caused drift in some runs). For teams aiming to reduce downstream reframing, a narrowly scoped, reproducible trial that targets Narrative while holding upstream inputs constant is the most defensible next step. By constraining which artifacts may be quoted and requiring artifact citations, the brief avoids inventing stage text and supports reproducible evaluation. Uncertainties to surface: Narrative may only reveal one pathway; Synthesis or Idea may still be root causes in other conditions; the trial must keep other variables fixed to avoid confounding.
evidence: Experiment 010 executive findings and cross‑experiment patterns: “Narrative is the most recurrent first visible hierarchy shift” and the per‑run localization tables showing Narrative as the earliest observable shift in multiple runs (Experiments 007–009). Implication for the next focused trial: Experiment 010 recommends “one controlled upstream‑boundary trial” targeting the stage supported by the evidence (Narrative) and lists separate evaluation axes (factual claims, hierarchy, editorial quality). The report includes an evidence‑manifest.json that must be used when extracting full stage outputs.

title: A Two‑Gate Review Framework: Separate Source Fidelity from Editorial Quality
description: Draft a practical two‑gate checklist and lightweight rubric to apply at Synthesis→Narrative and Narrative→Compose handoffs. Gate 1: Source/factual fidelity — verify each nontrivial claim against the reconstructed brief or preserved run artifacts; Gate 2: Editorial quality and hierarchy — confirm the lead is company‑first (when required), product as supporting direction, and that prose achieves opening interest and clarity. Provide clear examples of failure modes from Experiment 010 (using only quoted phrases preserved in the report) and recommend reproducible logging fields to capture gate decisions.
audience: Content QA engineers, reviewers, experiment evaluators, and prompt reviewers responsible for accept/reject decisions on generated company introductions.
rationale: Experiment 010 repeatedly separates factual and editorial failures: a description can be source‑aligned yet the wrong editorial lead, or editorially strong but factually unsupported. A two‑gate framework reduces false positives (factually true but wrong narrative lead) and false negatives (engaging text that invents claims). The framework should be applied with artifact‑backed checking to avoid inventing support for claims.
evidence: Executive findings: “Factual and editorial failures are distinct.” Cross‑experiment patterns: “Source fidelity and editorial quality need separate gates.” Report examples where Compose amplified upstream wording into stronger claims (e.g., “reliably converts,” “predictable and repeatable”) and where editorial framing (orchestration first) departed from company‑first intent.

title: Close Upstream Format Leakage: Audit Checklist and Controlled Removal Plan
description: Create an audit checklist to detect and remove explicit format/platform references from Idea/Research/Narrative system and user prompts that conflict with the Master Workflow’s format‑independence rule. The deliverable will (a) enumerate offending prompt fragments found in Experiment 010, (b) provide a minimal refactor pattern and a test that flags prompt text containing platform words (LinkedIn, Article, post, newsletter), and (c) specify a controlled test: run paired pipelines with and without the prompt references held equal elsewhere to measure any change in downstream format‑related drift. Require that any excerpted prompt text be cited to its prompt snapshot file path/hash from the report’s artifacts.
audience: Prompt engineers, workflow architects, and owners of Master Workflow system prompts.
rationale: Experiment 010 documents upstream prompts that include format references, calls this an “instruction‑boundary inconsistency,” and identifies it as a plausible confound for format priming. A conservative audit and a controlled removal test will reduce an avoidable source of priming while measuring whether it materially affects hierarchy or editorial outcomes. The intervention is expressly experimental, not claimed to be a universal cure.
evidence: Format‑agnostic architecture audit in Experiment 010 noting frozen Idea/Research/Narrative prompts containing 'supported output formats' and explicit Article/LinkedIn references; interpretation that this is a plausible source of format priming but not proven causation. The report’s recommendation to avoid upstream format‑aware decisions unless the hypothesis targets format leakage.

title: Reusable Experiment Template: Controlled Upstream‑Boundary Trial Manifest
description: Deliver a runnable experiment manifest and evaluation rubric that captures Experiment 010’s recommended controls: reconstructed source and execution settings identical, target Narrative with comparison to its input Synthesis, configuration option to remove format priming, repeated interleaved full‑pipeline runs, and three‑axis evaluation (factuality, hierarchy, editorial quality). Include example artifact paths, commands, the expected evidence‑manifest entries, and a configurable editorial scoring sheet. Make the template explicit that it is testing a hypothesis, not guaranteeing remediation.
audience: Experiment operators, data‑science teams, and product teams running Compose experiments who need a reproducible trial setup.
rationale: Experiment 010 gives a clear experimental design but no canned manifest. Packaging the design into an executable template reduces setup error, enforces artifact citation, and makes results comparable across iterations. The template should allow configurable pass thresholds for editorial quality because those remain subjective and under‑measured in prior runs.
evidence: Implication for the next focused trial: five numbered experimental controls in Experiment 010 (target stage, test rule, format‑priming handling, repeated runs with interleaving, separate evaluation axes). Repository context and evidence‑manifest.json existence support reproducibility needs.

title: How Compose Amplifies Upstream Framing — A Concise Diagnostic Taxonomy
description: Produce a short analytic note that categorizes observed Compose amplification behaviors with run‑level examples (inherit, amplify/add certainty, invent audiences, escalate scope). Use only the phrases and examples preserved in Experiment 010 (e.g., 'orchestration‑first,' 'reliably converts,' 'predictable and repeatable') and reference the per‑run localization tables to show where Compose inherited versus escalated wording. Conclude with suggested short checks to run before a Compose stage is accepted (e.g., flag certainty words, audience expansions, market‑generalizing phrases).
audience: Product managers, senior reviewers, and experiment evaluators who need a quick diagnostic to decide whether to change upstream prompts or Compose settings.
rationale: Experiment 010 includes direct observations that Compose can inherit, amplify, or add factual strength; a compact taxonomy makes it easier to triage whether a Compose fix suffices or upstream changes are required. Emphasize that these are observed patterns, not proven causal mechanisms, and tie each example back to preserved artifacts or the report tables.
evidence: Cross‑experiment observations: 'Compose can amplify, add factual strength, or simply inherit' and examples listed in the report ('orchestration‑first', 'reliably converts', 'predictable and repeatable'). Per‑run localization tables in Experiments 007–009 showing where Compose added or escalated claims.
